questions.stem: Which best describes the external environment of a business?
options: the factors inside the business that its managers can directly control
only the laws and regulations made by the various levels of government
only the customers who buy the business's goods and services
all the factors outside the business that may influence its operations
questions.explanation: The external environment includes everything outside the business that can act as a pressure or force on it, made up of the macro and operating environments. Factors managers can directly control, such as staffing and structure, form the internal environment.

questions.stem: How does the operating environment differ from the macro environment?
options: The operating environment contains only government laws; the macro environment contains only the business's customers and suppliers.
The operating environment is part of the internal environment; the macro environment includes everything outside the business.
The operating environment affects the business directly and it can be influenced; the macro environment is broader and largely beyond control.
The operating environment is broader and beyond the business's control; the macro environment is made up of the business's own staff and resources.
questions.explanation: Operating factors such as customers, competitors and suppliers affect a business directly, and the business can influence them to some degree. Macro factors such as the economy, society and global forces affect all businesses and are largely beyond any one business's control.

questions.stem: Which is a factor in the operating environment of a planned Ballarat bakery?
options: a rise in the national unemployment rate
a change to the company tax rate
a shift in Australians' attitudes to eating sugary foods
a nearby supermarket that starts baking its own bread
questions.explanation: A nearby supermarket baking bread is a competitor, which is part of the operating environment. Unemployment, tax rates and national attitudes are macro factors that affect all businesses, not just this bakery.

questions.stem: Which is a macro factor affecting a planned Adelaide furniture store?
options: a key timber supplier raising its prices
a competitor opening a showroom nearby
a local customer group asking for longer hours
a fall in consumer confidence across Australia
questions.explanation: Consumer confidence is an economic condition that affects spending throughout the economy, making it a macro factor. Suppliers, competitors and customers are part of the operating environment.

questions.stem: Before opening a café in Victoria, the owner must register the premises as a food business with:
options: the Reserve Bank of Australia
the Australian Securities and Investments Commission
the local council
the Fair Work Commission
questions.explanation: In Victoria, food premises are registered with the local council, which also inspects them for food safety. ASIC registers companies and business names but does not regulate food safety.

questions.stem: A planned panel-beating workshop is refused a site in a residential street because the area is not zoned for that use. This is an example of:
options: a societal attitude affecting where businesses are located
a supplier factor in the operating environment of the business
a technological consideration that affects business planning
a legal and government regulation affecting business planning
questions.explanation: Zoning rules set by state and local governments determine which activities can take place on a site, so they are legal and government regulations. They can force a business to change its planned location.

questions.stem: Why should a business owner understand the relevant legal and government regulations during the planning stage?
options: Regulations apply only to public listed companies and not to small businesses.
Once a bank approves the business plan, government regulations no longer apply.
Breaches can lead to fines or closure, and regulations can affect costs, location and timing.
Regulations apply only to businesses that have already been trading for at least twelve months.
questions.explanation: Laws and regulations apply from the start, and planning for them avoids penalties and unexpected costs or delays. Small businesses must meet the same legal requirements as large ones, such as licensing, zoning and consumer law.

questions.stem: A planned bar in Geelong needs a liquor licence, a planning permit and food premises registration before it can open. The most important planning implication is that:
options: only the liquor licence matters, because the other approvals are voluntary
the approvals can be avoided altogether if the bar is set up as a private limited company
the opening date and budget must allow for the time and cost of gaining approvals
the owner can open first and then apply for approvals once the bar is trading
questions.explanation: Approvals take time and money to obtain, and trading without them is illegal, so the plan's timeline and budget must include them. The business structure does not change the licences and permits a bar needs.

questions.stem: Societal attitudes and behaviour, as a macro factor, refers to:
options: the level of interest rates and consumer confidence in the economy
the actions of competitors operating in the same local market
the values, beliefs and trends of the community in which a business operates
the laws that parliament passes to regulate how businesses must operate
questions.explanation: Societal attitudes are the values, beliefs and trends of the community, such as concern for the environment or health. They shape what customers want and how they expect businesses to behave.

questions.stem: Growing concern about single-use plastics leads a planned Fremantle grocery store to build its shop around refill stations. The factor most influencing its planning is:
options: offshoring of labour
societal attitudes and values
changes in the exchange rate of the dollar
levels of employment
questions.explanation: The store is responding to a change in community values about waste, which is a societal attitude. The scenario does not involve the economy, overseas currencies or moving work overseas.

questions.stem: Which trend is most likely to create an opportunity for a planned plant-based food manufacturer?
options: rising consumer demand for cheaper cuts of beef, lamb and pork
a fall in the number of people eating at restaurants
falling consumer interest in health and nutrition
more consumers choosing to reduce the meat in their diets
questions.explanation: A shift towards eating less meat increases demand for plant-based alternatives, creating an opportunity. Rising demand for red meat or falling interest in health would work against such a business.

questions.stem: A new small business can influence some external factors but not others. Which external factor is it least able to influence?
options: the loyalty of its own regular customers
the terms it negotiates with its suppliers
its working relationship with the local traders' association
changing societal attitudes towards working from home
questions.explanation: Society-wide attitudes are macro factors, which a single small business cannot change. Customer loyalty, supplier terms and relationships with local associations are operating factors that the business can influence through its own actions.

questions.stem: Which economic condition is most likely to lead consumers to spend more?
options: rising unemployment
higher personal income tax rates
high consumer confidence
rising interest rates
questions.explanation: When consumers are confident about their jobs and the economy, they are more willing to spend. Rising interest rates, unemployment and income tax rates all reduce the money households have or are willing to spend.

questions.stem: Interest rates rise while a Sunshine Coast entrepreneur is planning to borrow $300,000 to start a business. The most direct effect on her plan is:
options: lower loan repayments, which would let her borrow more than she first planned
higher consumer spending, because savers will earn more interest
a guaranteed fall in competition, because rivals cannot borrow at all
higher loan repayments, which raise costs and may reduce what she borrows
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing, so the business's repayments and costs rise, and she may decide to borrow less. Higher rates usually reduce rather than increase consumer spending, because households with loans have less to spend.

questions.stem: A planned business will borrow $200,000 on an interest-only loan at 6% per year. If the interest rate rises to 7% per year, its annual interest cost rises by:
questions.explanation: Interest at 6% is 0.06 × $200,000 = $12,000 a year, and at 7% it is 0.07 × $200,000 = $14,000 a year. The increase is $14,000 − $12,000 = $2,000; $12,000 and $14,000 are the total costs, not the change.

questions.stem: Unemployment in a region is low. For a business planning to open there, the main implication for staffing is that:
options: it may be harder to recruit staff, and higher wages may be needed
it will find it easy to recruit staff at lower wages than usual
it will face weak demand, because few people in the area have incomes
it is legally required to employ its staff from outside the region
questions.explanation: When unemployment is low, fewer people are looking for work, so businesses compete for staff and may have to pay more. Low unemployment also means more people have incomes, which tends to support rather than weaken demand.

questions.stem: A cut in the company tax rate would most directly help a planned private limited company by:
options: increasing the after-tax profit it can reinvest or pay to shareholders
reducing the rate of GST that it must charge customers on each taxable sale
lowering the interest rate it is charged on its business loans
reducing the minimum wages it is required to pay its staff
questions.explanation: Company tax is paid on a company's profit, so a lower rate leaves more profit after tax to reinvest or distribute. GST, interest rates and minimum wages are set separately and are not changed by the company tax rate.

questions.stem: Consumer confidence falls sharply while two businesses are being planned: a premium car-detailing service and a discount grocery store. Which is likely to be affected more, and why?
options: the grocery store, because consumers stop buying food when they lose confidence
the car-detailing service, because spending on non-essential services is usually cut first
the grocery store, because confident consumers spend most of their income on essentials
both equally, because consumer confidence affects every kind of spending to the same degree
questions.explanation: When confidence falls, households cut back on discretionary spending such as premium services, while still buying essentials such as groceries. A discount grocer may even gain customers as shoppers look for lower prices.

questions.stem: Which is a technological consideration when planning a business?
options: the wage rates set in the modern award that covers the industry
how future developments may change the way customers buy products
the rate of company tax that is set by the federal government each year
the attitudes of local residents towards new developments
questions.explanation: Technological considerations include how the market may change with new technology and how the business will adapt to it. Tax rates and wage rates are economic and legal factors, and residents' attitudes are a societal factor.

questions.stem: A planned Canberra travel agency expects more customers to book trips themselves using apps. The best planning response is to:
options: offer services that apps cannot easily replace, such as complex tailored tours
ignore the trend, because changes in technology affect only very large national firms
rely only on walk-in customers, who are certain never to use booking apps
price every trip below cost so it can compete with free booking apps
questions.explanation: Adapting to technology means planning for how the market will change, for example by focusing on services where expert advice adds value. Ignoring the trend risks losing customers, and pricing below cost is not sustainable.

questions.stem: Why is technological change a risk as well as an opportunity for a business in the planning stage?
options: Equipment chosen now may soon be outdated, but new technology can also cut costs and reach new customers.
New technology always increases a business's costs and never improves its efficiency or its reach.
Technology affects only businesses that sell online, so bricks-and-mortar businesses can ignore it.
Technology can safely be ignored at the planning stage and considered only after trading begins.
questions.explanation: Technology can make a business more efficient and open new markets, but rapid change can make the systems a business invests in obsolete. Planning must weigh both, whether or not the business sells online.

questions.stem: Offshoring of labour means:
options: employing staff from overseas to work at the business's premises in Australia
hiring another Australian firm to do work the business used to do itself
selling goods made in Australia to customers living in other countries
moving some of a business's work, such as a call centre, to another country
questions.explanation: Offshoring relocates work to another country, usually to take advantage of lower labour costs. Contracting another Australian firm to do the work is outsourcing, and selling to overseas customers is exporting.

questions.stem: The Australian dollar rises in value against the US dollar. For an Australian wine exporter selling in the United States, this most likely means:
options: its sales are unaffected, because its prices are set in Australian dollars
its wine becomes dearer for US buyers, which may reduce its sales
its wine becomes cheaper for US buyers, which may increase its sales
the cost of any equipment it imports from the US rises sharply
questions.explanation: When the Australian dollar rises, US buyers need more US dollars to buy the same Australian-dollar price, so Australian exports become dearer. At the same time, imports from the US become cheaper for Australian businesses.

questions.stem: An Adelaide retailer imports goods priced at 6,000 US dollars. The exchange rate falls from 0.75 to 0.60 US dollars per Australian dollar. The cost of the goods in Australian dollars:
options: falls from $10,000 to $8,000
falls from $4,500 to $3,600
stays at $6,000 throughout
rises from $8,000 to $10,000
questions.explanation: The Australian-dollar cost is 6,000 ÷ 0.75 = $8,000 before and 6,000 ÷ 0.60 = $10,000 after. Multiplying by the exchange rate instead of dividing gives $4,500 and $3,600, which wrongly suggests a falling dollar makes imports cheaper.

questions.stem: Copyright in Australia:
options: must be registered with IP Australia before it can protect any work
protects ideas themselves, even if they are never written down or recorded in any form
protects inventions such as new machines and manufacturing processes
applies automatically when an original work is created, with no registration
questions.explanation: In Australia copyright protection arises automatically when an original work, such as writing, music, artwork or software code, is created in material form. Inventions are protected by patents, which must be applied for through IP Australia.

questions.stem: A Hobart start-up has designed a new type of solar water pump. To stop others making and selling the same design, it should apply for:
options: copyright
a trade mark
a business name
a patent
questions.explanation: A patent gives the owner the exclusive right to make, use and sell an invention for a limited period. A trade mark protects brand identifiers such as names and logos, not how a product works.

questions.stem: A planned skincare brand wants to stop competitors using a name and logo similar to its own. It should register:
options: a patent with IP Australia
its logo's copyright with IP Australia
its business name with the ATO
a trade mark with IP Australia
questions.explanation: Registering a trade mark with IP Australia gives the exclusive right to use the brand name and logo for the registered goods and services. Copyright cannot be registered in Australia, and business names are registered with ASIC, not the ATO.

questions.stem: Overseas competitors selling online to Australian customers mean that a planned local homewares store should most likely:
options: set its prices well above overseas sellers, because local goods always sell
avoid an online presence, so that customers do not compare it with others
plan to compete on service, range or convenience rather than on price alone
assume that Australian customers will not buy from overseas websites
questions.explanation: Overseas online sellers may have lower costs, so a local store needs advantages they cannot easily match, such as advice, quick delivery or the chance to see products. Australians do buy from overseas websites, so ignoring this competition would be risky.

questions.stem: Online sales let a small Bendigo leather-goods maker sell to customers overseas. Which planning issue does this raise most directly?
options: converting to a public listed company, which is required in order to trade overseas
abandoning the local market, because overseas sales must replace all local sales
managing international shipping costs, returns and changes in exchange rates
obtaining a patent for every product before it can be sold to overseas customers
questions.explanation: Selling overseas brings costs and risks such as freight, customs, handling returns from a distance and prices that shift with the exchange rate. A business of any structure can sell overseas, and patents are only relevant to inventions.

questions.stem: Planning for the socially responsible production of goods means:
options: choosing methods that avoid harm to workers, communities and the environment
producing goods at the lowest possible cost, regardless of who or what is affected
meeting only the minimum standards that are required by the law
producing goods that are to be sold only to charities and community groups
questions.explanation: Socially responsible production considers the effects of how goods are made on people and the environment, beyond what the law requires. Producing at the lowest cost regardless of the effects is the opposite of this approach.

questions.stem: A planned Victorian clothing label decides to use only factories that are independently audited for fair wages and safe conditions. Which is the most likely benefit?
options: lower production costs than labels that use unaudited factories
an exemption from the requirements of the Australian Consumer Law
a guarantee that the label will never face criticism of any kind
a stronger reputation with customers who value ethical production
questions.explanation: Ethical sourcing can build trust and loyalty with customers who care how their clothes are made. It usually raises rather than lowers costs, and it does not change the business's legal obligations.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur planning a car wash chooses a water-recycling system that costs $40,000 more than a standard system. Which statement best evaluates this CSR decision?
options: It will reduce the business's profit in every single year that the car wash operates.
It guarantees the car wash will attract more customers than every one of its rivals.
It is irrelevant to planning, because CSR applies only to large public companies.
It raises start-up costs but may lower water bills and appeal to environmentally aware customers.
questions.explanation: A balanced evaluation weighs the higher initial cost against ongoing savings and the reputational benefit of reducing water use. The savings may outweigh the cost over time, so it will not necessarily reduce profit every year.

questions.stem: Customers' needs and expectations affect business planning because:
options: customers set the maximum prices that a business is legally allowed to charge
customers decide the legal structure that the business must adopt
customers are part of the internal environment controlled by managers
a business must offer what its target customers want if it is to make sales
questions.explanation: A business only succeeds if customers buy from it, so its products, prices and service must be planned around what its target customers need and expect. Customers are part of the operating environment, not the internal environment.

questions.stem: Customers of a planned Sydney dental clinic expect online booking and text-message reminders. The clinic's plan should therefore:
options: rely on phone bookings only, since customers will adapt to the clinic
set higher fees, since expectations always increase customer spending
ignore these expectations until a competing clinic offers online booking
include booking systems that meet these expectations before it opens
questions.explanation: Meeting customer expectations from the start helps the clinic attract and keep patients. Waiting until a competitor acts would risk losing customers to clinics that already offer what patients expect.

questions.stem: Why should a business analyse its competitors' behaviour when planning?
options: to decide how it will differentiate itself and price its products
so that it can copy every feature of its competitors' products exactly
because competitors must formally approve its business plan
because competitors are part of its own internal environment
questions.explanation: Knowing what competitors offer and charge helps a business find a point of difference and set competitive prices. Competitors are part of the operating environment and have no role in approving another firm's plans.

questions.stem: A new gym is preparing to open in Toowoomba. Two weeks before its opening, an established rival cuts its membership fees by 30%. This is an example of:
options: a legal regulation in the macro environment
a supplier factor in the operating environment
competitors' behaviour in the operating environment
economic conditions in the macro environment
questions.explanation: A rival changing its prices is competitors' behaviour, an operating factor that directly affects the new gym. Economic conditions such as interest rates affect all businesses, whereas this action targets the same local market.

questions.stem: A planned café would be the only one in a new housing estate, but a national chain announces it will open nearby. The best planning response is to:
options: keep the plan unchanged, because customers always stay with whichever café opens first
identify features the chain cannot easily match, such as local produce and personal service
set its prices below cost from the first day until the chain decides to close its store
abandon the plan, because a small business is never able to compete with a chain
questions.explanation: Small businesses can compete with chains by offering a point of difference, such as local character, flexibility or personal service. Pricing below cost cannot be sustained, and many small cafés trade successfully alongside chains.

questions.stem: A business's supply chain is:
options: the chain of command running from the owner down to the most junior staff member
the list of customers who regularly buy goods and services from the business
the group of businesses that operate together within a single franchise network
the steps and businesses involved in getting resources to it and products to customers
questions.explanation: The supply chain covers where resources come from, how they reach the business and how finished products reach customers. The chain of command describes management structure, not the flow of goods.

questions.stem: A planned Darwin restaurant will rely on one interstate supplier for all of its fresh seafood. The main risk is that:
options: the restaurant will need to hold a patent for each of its seafood dishes
customers will refuse to eat any seafood that has come from interstate
a delay or failure at that one supplier could stop the restaurant operating
the supplier will become legally entitled to set all of the restaurant's menu prices
questions.explanation: Depending on a single, distant supplier leaves the restaurant exposed if deliveries are delayed or the supplier fails. Using several suppliers or local sources would reduce this supply chain risk.

questions.stem: A Melbourne electronics retailer can source a product locally in 3 days for $50 a unit, or from overseas in 6 weeks for $35 a unit. Which statement best evaluates the overseas option?
options: It lowers the unit cost but increases the risk of stock shortages and exchange-rate changes.
It is always better, because buying at the lowest unit cost always maximises the profit.
It removes any need to hold stock, because overseas delivery times are guaranteed.
It reduces supply risk, because goods coming from further away are more reliable.
questions.explanation: The overseas supplier is cheaper per unit, but long lead times make it harder to respond to demand, and the price in Australian dollars will change with the exchange rate. A lower unit cost does not maximise profit if sales are lost through shortages.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a special interest group?
options: the business's largest regular customer
a competitor in the same shopping strip
the bank that lends money to the business
a trade union representing hospitality workers
questions.explanation: Special interest groups, such as unions, environmental lobby groups and business associations, try to influence businesses and governments on behalf of their members or causes. Customers, competitors and lenders are other parts of the operating environment.

questions.stem: An environmental lobby group campaigns against a planned resort beside a coastal wetland in Queensland. The most likely effect on the resort's planning is:
options: delays and pressure to change the design to reduce environmental harm
a legal obligation to transfer ownership of the resort to the lobby group
lower building costs, because the lobby group will help fund the project
an automatic ban, imposed by the group, on the resort hiring any staff
questions.explanation: Lobby groups can raise public concern and press governments, which may delay approvals or lead the business to change its plans. A lobby group has no legal power to take ownership of a business or control its hiring.

questions.stem: A planned retailer joins its local traders' association. How might this business association affect its planning?
options: It can formally approve or refuse each member's business plan before trading begins.
It controls which suppliers its member businesses are permitted to buy stock from.
It can provide information and represent members' interests to councils and governments.
It can set the legal minimum wages that each of its members is required to pay their staff.
questions.explanation: Business associations share information, run networking events and lobby on behalf of their members, for example about parking or council rates. Minimum wages are set through the Fair Work system, not by business associations.
